messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The attack happened eight months ago, in the apartment he shared with his girlfriend at the time. Ravi had finally told her he wanted to end things. She laughed, then slapped him. When he didn’t react, she hit him again, harder, her fists coming down on his chest and face as he lay on the floor. He remembers the sour smell of her sweat as she leaned over him, the way her body blocked the light. He did nothing—he didn’t push her off, didn’t shout, didn’t leave. He lay still and waited for it to stop. That stillness, that absence of action, is what he cannot live with.

In the months after, Ravi’s convenience store became a minefield. The first time a customer walked in after a summer run, the sharp tang of body odour hit him and his heart seized—his eyes locked on the exit, certain that something terrible was about to happen again (Triggers → Threat). That same smell, without any warning, would also drag the full memory back: the thud of her fists, the humiliation, and a wave of rage so sudden it made his hands shake (Triggers → Memory). Sometimes the emotion came without any clear image—just the raw feeling of helplessness and fury, and he would stand behind the counter gripping the edge until it passed. Afterward, he would tell himself that his body was betraying him again, reacting to nothing, and that he could not rely on himself to stay calm (Triggers → Negative Appraisals). The belief that he was fundamentally weak and passive hardened. “I will never forgive myself for not doing more,” he thought, and that guilt burrowed deeper.

That guilt and the idea that his body was his enemy began to shape everything. Because he saw his own reactions as proof that danger was everywhere, he started feeling threatened by strangers even in ordinary situations—a man walking toward him on the sidewalk, a customer who stood too close (Negative Appraisals → Threat). At night, alone in his apartment, the threat felt constant; his sleep fractured, his ears straining for footsteps or voices. The memory, whenever it surfaced, reinforced the guilt and the sense of being powerless: each intrusive recall of his inaction made him feel more certain that he had failed, that he could not trust himself (Memory → Negative Appraisals). And the rage that accompanied the memory—intense, hot—left him feeling unsafe, as if he might lose control and do something violent himself (Memory → Threat).

The more he believed he was unreliable, the more he watched for triggers. He began to notice his own sweat during anxious moments, and the scent would instantly transport him back to that apartment, confirming again that his body was an enemy (Negative Appraisals → Triggers). At work, he would overhear customers arguing or talking about relationships, and those conversation topics would set off the same cascade—first the memory, then the guilt, then the feeling that he was still in danger. His constant vigilance itself pulled triggers into focus: the state of scanning for threats meant that any hint of a smell or a raised voice registered as a signal (Threat → Triggers). He started closing the shop earlier, avoiding the evening hours when his fear peaked. His current girlfriend noticed how jumpy he had become, how he flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind, how he refused to go out after dark. She asked him what was wrong, but he couldn’t explain.

What brought Ravi to therapy was the exhaustion. The cycle had tightened until he was living from trigger to trigger, never feeling safe, never trusting his own mind. He was tired of the nightly watchfulness, tired of the rage that came without warning. But what frightened him most was the thought that he might never stop feeling weak, that he would always be the person who froze. He hoped that if he could somehow understand why his body still reacts, he might finally forgive himself for doing nothing.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals (e.g., 'I am weak') cause the trauma memory to surface; instead, the memory is triggered by external cues.
The vignette does not show that the trauma memory leads to increased awareness or detection of triggers; vigilance is linked to threat and negative appraisals instead.
